title: Letter 21 — Thou Shalt Not Steal
attribution_note: Letter 21 of 46 in the collection Letters Sent — see Letter 1 for provenance.

pairs.en: You wish to know from me what this word means: *“Thou shalt not steal”* [Exodus 20:15], and you ask for an explanation of it.

Answer. Short is this word, yet it spreads wide, and many offend against it: some from inattention and ignorance, others from shamelessness and lawless will — which is heavier than the first. Attend, then, how theft or robbery spreads abroad:

1) Theft known to all — as when men secretly rob shops, granaries and the rest, or by force seize what is another's, as robbers do, or the powerful who are fearless and without conscience. Of such robbery everyone knows — even the roughest men who know not the Scriptures, and even the youngest and smallest children.
2) Theft and robbery — when judges and officers of the court judge for a bribe, and not according to the Christian duty.

3) Theft and robbery — when landlords burden their peasants with excessive dues or labours, since they take from them what is needful for their sustenance and the support of their life and of their household. And this is a fierce and inhuman robbery, though men do not mark it. The poor peasant toils and sweats the whole summer through, yet has nothing with which to feed and clothe himself and his household. One master devours all. Woe to such masters! They cause as many tears to be shed as the excess they lay upon the peasants. God, the Righteous Judge, sees these tears and those who shed them.
4) Theft and robbery — when hirelings are not paid in full, or are not paid at all. And this too is a fierce and inhuman robbery, for the poor man is wronged.

sections.heading: Hirelings and servants that will not work

pairs.en: 5) Theft and robbery — when hirelings, having taken a just price, either do not work, or work slothfully.
6) Theft and robbery — when servants receive from their masters wages or sustenance, yet either work slothfully, or do not work at all.

7) Theft and robbery — when a ruler withholds from a subordinate his wages, or does not give them in full, without any cause, and appropriates them to himself. And this is a fierce robbery, for the poor man is wronged.
8) Theft and robbery — when a merchant sells a bad thing for a good, and a cheap for a dear, or mixes water with wine and sells it as pure wine.
9) Theft and robbery — when a man deliberately fattens horses or other cattle that are weak and poor, so as to sell them for sound, and thus deceive the buyers.

10) Theft and robbery — playing at cards for money; for he who wins sins against the commandment: *“Thou shalt not steal.”* And he who does not win, though he lose all his substance and even himself, also steals by his own will; for he desires another's goods, and sins against the commandment of God: *“Thou shalt not covet”* [Exodus 20:17]. Likewise everyone who desires to seize and appropriate another's thing, though he do not seize it in the deed itself, is a robber; for a man sins or does not sin by his will. And such a man, who desires another's goods, already steals by his will, though he should not steal in the deed; for sin consists in the will and free choice of man. When a man wills to seize what is another's, he already seizes it by his will; he wills to commit fornication, and already commits fornication; he wills to kill a man, and already has killed by his will.

But if there is no sin in the will, then neither is there any in the deed itself. When a man's will is good, the man too is good; and when the will is evil, the man too is evil. By his will each one is either evil or good. Thus a man is evil who has an evil will, though he should not do outward evil deeds. In the will and heart of man dwells the murderer, the fornicator, the thief, and every other evil. And what is not in the heart is not in the deed itself. The will and the heart must be corrected, and then the man will be good.

11) Robbery — when a master seeks and asks some thing of a slave or peasant, and a ruler of one under his power. For the subordinate cannot dispute with the ruler, and therefore even unwillingly gives what he asks; he is compelled and gives against his will, and not by free consent. Rightly do learned men teach: when superiors ask of inferiors, they command.

12) Robbery and theft — when one takes from another money, or any other thing, for safekeeping, or in pledge, and does not return it, and says either that he has returned it, or that he never took it.
13) Robbery — when one takes something on loan and returns to the lender neither that thing nor anything else in its place.
14) Robbery — when one takes from another money or anything else for the giving of alms, and keeps it for himself, or puts it to some other use.
15) Robbery — when one finds a lost thing and does not make it known, but keeps it for himself.

16) To robbery belongs usury, or interest; and the fiercest robbery is when it is taken from the poor — for thus the naked is stripped bare, and the powerless is brought into greater powerlessness; whereas such a one, by Christian love, ought to be helped without return.

17) To robbery it belongs when men, feigning themselves beggars though they have wherewith to live, or feigning themselves infirm though they are whole, ask alms, so that men may help them by the giving of alms — the one as if infirm, the other as if poor and without sustenance.
18) Robbery — when carts and conveyance are taken by craft, and without the lawful price.
19) Robbery — when a servant will not admit to his master a man who comes, without money, and seeks to take money from him for the audience.
20) Robbery — when one, not willing to labour, though he is whole, goes about from house to house and eats another's bread.

sections.heading: Wealth shut up from the poor

pairs.en: 21) Robbery is this also: when a rich man holds the wealth given him by God either locked up, or squanders it on unprofitable expenses, and does not share with the poor as a Christian ought. For God gives wealth to men not for their own sake alone, but also for the sake of the poor and needy. *“If any one,”* says Saint Basil the Great, *“strips a man of his garment, he is called a ruffian and a thief.* *Is not he who fails to clothe the naked, when he is able to do so, a greater ruffian and thief?* *The bread of the hungry is that bread which is with you; the clothing of the naked is that which you keep in your chest; the shoes of the barefoot are those which rot with you; the silver of the poor is that which you keep buried in the earth.* *Behold how many men you wrong, when, being able, you render no assistance”* (Discourse on Almsgiving). Let the miserly and the rich who live in luxury consider this, and attend to what is written (see Matthew 25:41–46).
22) You see how many kinds of robbery there are. From these, know also the other kinds of robbery, which I have not touched upon here.
23) From this you see how many thieves and robbers there are in the world!

24) If any one wishes to keep himself from robbery, and not to be condemned as a robber at the Dread Judgment, he must correct himself and attend to the universal rule: what you would not have done to yourself, do not to your neighbour; and what you would have done to yourself, do to your neighbour (see Acts 15:20, 29). To this the law of God and the holy prophets, and our blessed Fathers, and the teachers of the Church, instruct.
Save thyself.
